title: The conclave
hookLine: cardinals under eighty lock themselves in the Sistine Chapel and vote until white smoke

cards: The doors of the Sistine Chapel are about to close, and a voice calls out two Latin words: extra omnes. Everyone out. Staff, cameras, guards: out.
Inside, under the painted ceiling, sit the cardinals who are allowed to vote. Their phones are gone. No news, no messages in or out.

They will stay inside this closed world, praying and voting, until one name has enough votes to make a pope. Outside, a crowd in Saint Peter's Square stares at a thin metal chimney on the chapel roof, waiting for smoke.

teach.h: UNDER EIGHTY, SWORN, AND LOCKED IN.
teach.b: Conclave names both the gathering and the locked-in way it works. Today's rules come from a document John Paul the Second wrote on electing a pope, later adjusted by Benedict.
Only cardinals under eighty may vote, and they swear to keep everything secret. The ballot is a card printed with the Latin for I elect as Supreme Pontiff, and a blank line.
Each cardinal writes one name, in handwriting meant to be hard to recognize.

teach.h: AN OATH AT THE ALTAR, CHRIST AS WITNESS.
teach.b: One at a time, he carries his folded card to the altar, beneath the great painting of the Last Judgment, and says an oath aloud: he calls Christ the Lord, who will be his judge, to witness that he is voting for the one he believes, before God, should be chosen.
It takes two-thirds of the votes to elect. After the counting, the ballots are burned in a stove.
Black smoke means no one yet.
White smoke, with the bells of Saint Peter's, means a pope, and a cardinal steps onto the balcony to announce: habemus papam, we have a pope. The Church sees something old in this.
In the Acts of the Apostles, before choosing someone to take the place of Judas, the apostles pray to the Lord who knows every heart and ask him to show whom he has chosen. Then they cast lots.
The conclave keeps the prayer and trades the lots for ballots: human votes, counted carefully, held inside prayer.
And this week's popes, the one who stepped down and the one from Buenos Aires, each walked out of this room.

how: When the papacy is vacant, Catholics around the world pray at Mass for the cardinals in conclave, and crowds gather in Saint Peter's Square to watch the chimney for white smoke.

games.q: you're a cardinal in the Sistine Chapel, folded card in hand, walking to the altar. what do you do?
o: drop it in without a word.
say an oath, calling Christ as witness that you vote for the one God would choose.
read the name aloud so everyone knows.
games.why: each cardinal says the oath aloud before casting his ballot. the name itself stays secret.

practice: Take one choice in front of you into a closed room: no phone, no polls. Hold up each option, one at a time, the way a cardinal carries his card to the altar, and notice which one you could carry with a clear conscience.
If you pray, ask, as the apostles did, to be shown the way; you don't have to decide yet, and black smoke is allowed.

wordCard.voice: Conclave. The locked gathering of cardinals that elects a pope, voting in the Sistine Chapel until one name has two-thirds of the votes.

orig.note: Latin: we have a pope, the words announced from the balcony after the white smoke.

carryVoice: Your line: white smoke. A decision, made and announced. See you tomorrow.
